modules.title: Introduction to Electromagnetism & Forces in Nature
modules.content:
The Four Fundamental Forces

Every force in nature belongs to one of these four categories:

  • Gravitational Force: Weakest force, acts between any two bodies due to mass. Keeps us attached to Earth.
  • Electromagnetic Force: Responsible for attraction/repulsion of charges and magnetic effects. Most everyday forces (except gravity) are electromagnetic.
  • Strong Nuclear Force: Holds protons and neutrons together in atomic nucleus. Powers the sun through nuclear fusion.
  • Weak Nuclear Force: Responsible for Beta decay (neutron → proton + electron).

Classical vs Modern Physics: Classical physics (what you're learning) describes matter and fields completely enough for engineering. Modern physics (Relativity + Quantum Theory) emerged in the 20th century for atomic-scale phenomena.
modules.feynman_prompt: Explain the difference between the four fundamental forces to a 10-year-old using a simple analogy.

flashcards.definition: The force responsible for attraction/repulsion of electric charges and magnetic effects. Most everyday forces are electromagnetic in nature.
The complete picture of matter and fields that includes electric and magnetic fields. Sufficient for many engineering applications.
The force that holds protons and neutrons together in the atomic nucleus, overpowering electromagnetic repulsion between protons.

micro_quiz.question: Which fundamental force is responsible for keeping electrons bound to the atomic nucleus?
micro_quiz.explanation: The electromagnetic force causes the attraction between the positively charged protons in the nucleus and the negatively charged electrons.

micro_quiz.question: True or False: Gravitational force is the strongest of the four fundamental forces.
micro_quiz.explanation: Gravitational force is actually the WEAKEST of the four fundamental forces, despite being the most noticeable in daily life.

modules.title: Electric Charge & Its Properties
modules.content:
What is Electric Charge?

Electric charge is a fundamental physical quantity of matter that causes it to experience a force when placed in an electric field.

Key Properties:

  1. Quantization: Charge exists in discrete units. The elementary charge e ≈ 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C. All charges are integer multiples: q = ne (where n = 0, ±1, ±2...)
  2. Conservation: Total charge in an isolated system remains constant. Charge cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.
  3. Attraction & Repulsion: Like charges repel (+/+ or -/-), unlike charges attract (+/-).
  4. Additivity: Total charge is the algebraic sum of all individual charges.

The Numbers:

  • Electron charge: -e = -1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C
  • Proton charge: +e = +1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C
  • Electron mass: m = 9.1094×10⁻³¹ kg
modules.feynman_prompt: Explain why charge is 'quantized' using a simple real-world analogy (like money or building blocks).

flashcards.definition: The smallest unit of electric charge: e ≈ 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ Coulombs. All free particles have charges that are integer multiples of this value.
The principle that electric charge exists only in discrete units (multiples of e), not continuous values.
The total electric charge in an isolated system remains constant over time. Charge can be transferred but never created or destroyed.
Conductors allow charge to move freely (metals). Insulators resist charge movement (rubber, glass, plastic).

micro_quiz.question: If you remove 1000 electrons from a neutral object, what is its net charge?
micro_quiz.explanation: Removing electrons (negative charge) leaves a positive charge. Q = 1000 × (+1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C) = +1.602×10⁻¹⁶ C

micro_quiz.question: Two objects have charges of +3e and -5e. What is the total charge of the system?

modules.title: Charging Methods: Friction, Conduction, Induction
modules.content:
Three Ways to Charge Objects:

1. Friction (Rubbing)

Transferring electrons between materials by rubbing them together. Example: Rubbing a plastic rod with fur transfers electrons from fur to plastic, making the plastic negatively charged.

2. Conduction (Direct Contact)

Transferring charge by direct contact between a charged and uncharged object. Electrons flow from one to the other until equilibrium is reached.

3. Induction (No Contact)

Separating charge within an object by bringing a charged object NEARBY, WITHOUT direct contact. The charged object polarizes the neutral object, then grounding one side creates a net charge.

Key Observation: Objects charged the same way REPEL each other. Objects charged differently ATTRACT each other.
modules.feynman_prompt: Describe the difference between charging by conduction and charging by induction using a simple analogy.

flashcards.definition: Transfer of electrons between materials through rubbing. The material that gains electrons becomes negative; the one that loses electrons becomes positive.
Transfer of charge through direct contact between charged and uncharged objects. Both objects end up with the same type of charge.
Charging without direct contact. A charged object polarizes a neutral object, and grounding creates a net charge opposite to the inducing charge.

micro_quiz.question: When you rub a glass rod with silk, the glass becomes positively charged. What happened?
options: Electrons moved from glass to silk
Electrons moved from silk to glass
Protons moved from silk to glass
Protons moved from glass to silk
micro_quiz.explanation: The glass lost electrons to the silk, leaving it with a net positive charge. Remember: only electrons move, protons stay in the nucleus!

modules.title: Coulomb's Law
modules.content:
Coulomb's Law Statement:

The force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

F = k|q₁q₂| / r²

Where:

  • k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C² (Coulomb's constant)
  • ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² C²/N·m² (permittivity of free space)
  • k = 1/(4πε₀)

Key Points:

  • Same sign charges (both + or both -): Force is REPULSIVE
  • Opposite sign charges (+ and -): Force is ATTRACTIVE
  • Superposition Principle: For multiple charges, the total force on one charge is the VECTOR SUM of all individual Coulomb forces from other charges.
modules.feynman_prompt: Explain why Coulomb's law has an 'inverse square' relationship (1/r²) rather than just 1/r. Use gravity as an analogy if helpful.

flashcards.definition: k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C². Also expressed as k = 1/(4πε₀), where ε₀ is the permittivity of free space.
When multiple charges are present, the total force on any one charge is the vector sum of all individual forces from all other charges.
The force decreases with the square of distance. Double the distance = 1/4 the force. Triple the distance = 1/9 the force.

micro_quiz.question: Two charges +3μC and -2μC are 0.1m apart. What is the magnitude of force between them? (k = 9×10⁹ N·m²/C²)
micro_quiz.explanation: F = k|q₁q₂|/r² = (9×10⁹)(3×10⁻⁶)(2×10⁻⁶)/(0.1)² = 54×10⁻³/0.01 = 5.4 N. The force is attractive since charges are opposite.

micro_quiz.question: If you double the distance between two charges, what happens to the force?
micro_quiz.explanation: Since F ∝ 1/r², doubling r means F becomes 1/(2²) = 1/4 of the original force.

modules.title: Electric Field
modules.content:
What is an Electric Field?

The electric field E at a point is the force per unit charge that would be exerted on a test charge placed at that point.

E = F/Q or F = QE

For a Point Charge:

E(r) = (1/4πε₀) × (q/r²) r̂

Where r̂ is the unit vector pointing radially outward from the charge.

Key Properties:

  • Vector Quantity: Has both magnitude and direction
  • Function of Position: Varies from point to point
  • Direction: Points AWAY from positive charges, TOWARD negative charges
  • Continuous Distribution: For line, surface, or volume charges, we integrate: E = ∫(1/4πε₀)(dq/r²)r̂
modules.feynman_prompt: Explain the difference between electric force and electric field. Why do we need the concept of 'field'?

flashcards.definition: A vector field that represents the force per unit charge at every point in space. E = F/Q, measured in N/C or V/m.
A hypothetical small positive charge used to map out the electric field. It must be small enough not to disturb the source charges.
Electric field lines point AWAY from positive charges and TOWARD negative charges.

micro_quiz.question: A +2μC charge experiences a force of 6N in an electric field. What is the field strength?

modules.title: Electric Potential
modules.content:
Electric Potential (Voltage)

The electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point.

V(r) = (1/4πε₀) × (Q/r) = kQ/r

Key Concepts:

  • Scalar Quantity: Unlike electric field, potential has no direction (just magnitude)
  • Path Independent: Work done depends only on start and end points, not the path taken
  • Work Done: W = qV (work to bring charge q to potential V)
  • Unit: Volt (V) = Joule/Coulomb

Example: For Q = 4×10⁻⁷ C at r = 9cm: V = (9×10⁹)(4×10⁻⁷)/0.09 = 4×10 V
modules.feynman_prompt: Explain the difference between electric potential (voltage) and electric potential energy using a gravity analogy.

flashcards.definition: Work done per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity to a point. V = kQ/r. Measured in Volts (J/C).
The energy a charge possesses due to its position in an electric field. U = qV.
The work done per unit charge in moving between two points. Also called voltage.

micro_quiz.question: How much work is done bringing a 3×10⁻⁹ C charge from infinity to a point where the potential is 5000V?

modules.title: Gauss's Law
modules.content:
Gauss's Law Statement:

The electric flux through any closed surface is proportional to the total charge enclosed by the surface.

Φ = Q/ε₀

Where:

  • Φ = electric flux through the closed surface
  • Q = net charge enclosed
  • ε₀ = permittivity of free space

Why Gauss's Law is Useful:

It provides a simpler method to determine electric fields for symmetric charge distributions (spheres, cylinders, planes) compared to Coulomb's law integration.

Electric Flux:

Flux measures how much electric field 'flows' through a surface: dΦ = E·dS (dot product of field and area vector).
modules.feynman_prompt: Explain Gauss's Law using a water flow analogy. What does 'flux' mean in this context?

flashcards.definition: The electric flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀: Φ = Q/ε₀
A measure of the electric field passing through a surface. Φ = ∫E·dS. Measured in N·m²/C.
An imaginary closed surface chosen to exploit symmetry when applying Gauss's Law to calculate electric fields.

micro_quiz.question: A sphere encloses a charge of +6μC. What is the total electric flux through the sphere? (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C²/N·m²)

modules.title: Problem Solving & Applications
modules.content:
Worked Examples from Module:

Example 1: Total Charge of Electrons

Problem: What is the total charge of 75.0 kg of electrons?

Solution:

  • Number of electrons: N = M/mₑ = 75.0/(9.11×10⁻³¹) = 8.23×10³¹
  • Total charge: Q = N(-e) = (8.23×10³¹)(-1.602×10⁻¹⁹) = -1.32×10¹³ C

Example 2: Nuclear Fission Force

Problem: Uranium-238 splits into two spheres, each with 46 protons and radius 5.9×10⁻¹⁵ m. Find the repulsive force.

Solution:

  • Charge per sphere: q = 46e = 7.37×10¹⁸ C
  • Separation: r = 2R = 1.18×10⁻¹⁴ m
  • Force: F = kq²/r² = 3.5×10³ N (repulsive)
modules.feynman_prompt: Walk through one complete problem from start to finish, explaining each step as if teaching someone who has never seen it before.

flashcards.definition: 1. Identify known quantities. 2. Identify what you're solving for. 3. Choose the appropriate formula. 4. Check units. 5. Solve algebraically first, then substitute numbers.

micro_quiz.question: A penny (3.11g of copper) is given a charge of +1.0×10⁷ C. What fraction of its electrons were removed? (Copper has 29 electrons per atom, atomic weight 63.54 g/mol)
micro_quiz.explanation: Electrons removed: 6.2×10¹¹. Total electrons in penny: 8.55×10²³. Fraction: 6.2×10¹¹/8.55×10²³ = 7.3×10⁻¹³ (an incredibly tiny fraction!)
